subject: use-of-english
title: Passage A
text: Adura had learned to read the room before she learned to read words. She watched the shoulders of her father when the letters from the bank arrived, and she knew before the envelope was opened that the answer would be no. By twelve she could tell which of her parents' silences meant anger and which meant simply tiredness, and she had already decided that growing up meant becoming the person who asked the questions nobody else thought to ask. It was not curiosity that drove her, exactly. It was the suspicion that adults were accustomed to a version of events that did not survive being examined too closely.

subject: use-of-english
title: The Lekki Headmaster
author: D. O. Fagunwa
text: The principal was not an unkind man, but he believed that the business of a school was discipline before it was instruction, and that a boy who had been properly taught to hold his tongue would learn more in a year than one who had been permitted to argue with his teacher. In this he was consistent to the point of severity, and the whole school understood that the first law of the assembly hall was silence, and the second was attention.

subject: use-of-english
title: Passage B
text: The boy was born before his parents actually got married and so the court had declared him .... Within a year the family had left the village, and by the time he was old enough to ask questions of his own he had learned that there were things about his own beginnings that adults preferred to discuss in a lowered voice.
